stages.title: Security Foundations
stages.description: The core vocabulary of defensive security: the CIA triad, how threats, vulnerabilities and risk relate, and the principles of defense in depth and least privilege.
learningObjectives: Define confidentiality, integrity and availability and give a control that protects each
Distinguish a threat, a vulnerability, impact/likelihood and risk
Explain defense in depth as layered, overlapping controls
Apply the principle of least privilege to user and process access

explainBack.question: Using the CIA triad, explain what security is trying to protect, how a threat, a vulnerability and risk relate to each other, and why defenders use defense in depth and least privilege.
rubric: Confidentiality keeps data private from unauthorized parties (e.g. encryption, MFA); integrity keeps data accurate and untampered (e.g. hashing, digital signatures); availability keeps systems usable when needed (e.g. backups, redundancy)
A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat actor can exploit (or a hazard can affect); a threat is someone or something with the capability and intent to cause harm
Risk is the possibility of something bad happening, weighed by likelihood and impact; it cannot be eliminated, only managed (avoid, accept, mitigate or transfer)
Defense in depth layers multiple people, technology and operations controls so an attack missed by one layer can be caught by another
Least privilege restricts each user or process to the minimum access needed to perform its assigned tasks

resources.title: The CIA Triad - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 1.2
resources.description: A short Security+ lesson introducing confidentiality, integrity and availability as the three goals of information security.
keyPoints: Defines confidentiality, integrity and availability
Gives examples of how each goal is protected
Part of a free full Security+ SY0-701 course

resources.title: Cybersecurity Architecture: Five Principles to Follow (and One to Avoid)
resources.description: An IBM security architect walks through core design principles such as defense in depth and least privilege, plus a common anti-pattern to avoid.
keyPoints: Covers defense in depth as layered protection
Covers the principle of least privilege
Also names one approach the presenter says to avoid

resources.title: What is the CIA Triad and Why is it important?
resources.description: Defines each part of the CIA triad and lists typical threats and controls for confidentiality, integrity and availability.
keyPoints: Confidentiality: keep data private; controls include encryption, MFA, access restrictions
Integrity: data stays trustworthy; controls include hashing, digital signatures, checksums
Availability: systems work when needed; threats include DoS and ransomware
Availability controls include redundancy, failover, disaster recovery and backups

resources.title: The fundamentals and basics of cyber risk
resources.description: NCSC's plain-language grounding in risk: what risk, threat, vulnerability, impact and likelihood mean and how organisations manage risk.
keyPoints: Risk: 'the possibility of something bad happening'
Vulnerability: any weakness a threat actor can exploit or a hazard can affect
Threats are characterised by capability, intent, motivation and opportunity
Risk can't be eliminated, only managed: avoid, accept, mitigate or transfer
Compliance with standards does not by itself equal good security

resources.title: defense-in-depth - Glossary | CSRC
resources.description: NIST's official glossary definitions of defense in depth, drawn from several NIST and ISO/IEC publications.
keyPoints: Strategy integrating people, technology and operations capabilities
Establishes barriers across multiple layers of the organization
Layers different technologies so attacks missed by one are caught by another

resources.title: least privilege - Glossary | CSRC
resources.description: NIST's official glossary definitions of the least privilege principle.
keyPoints: Restrict users, and processes acting for them, to the minimum access needed
Each entity gets only the minimum resources and authorizations for its function
Definitions sourced from CNSSI 4009, SP 800-53 Rev. 5 and SP 800-171r3

stages.title: Authentication & Passwords
stages.description: How modern authentication works and is defended: current NIST password rules, password managers, multifactor authentication, passkeys and credential stuffing.
learningObjectives: State current NIST SP 800-63B password rules (length, no composition rules, no forced periodic changes, blocklists)
Name the three authentication factor categories and explain why phishing-resistant MFA is strongest
Explain how a password manager and passkeys reduce password reuse and phishing
Describe credential stuffing and the defenses against it

explainBack.question: A friend reuses one 8-character password everywhere and changes it every 90 days. Explain what current guidance recommends instead, and why MFA and passkeys matter.
rubric: NIST SP 800-63B (Rev. 4) requires at least 15 characters for a password used alone (8 if only used within MFA), forbids composition rules and forbids forced periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise

Credential stuffing tests username/password pairs leaked from one site against other sites, so reusing passwords lets one breach unlock many accounts; a password manager makes unique passwords practical
MFA combines factors from different categories: something you know, something you have, something you are
Phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO/WebAuthn is strongest because it blocks logins to fake sites; SMS and push codes can be phished
A passkey is a FIDO credential: the private key stays on the user's device and only a public key is held by the site, so there is no shared secret to phish or leak

resources.title: Multifactor Authentication - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 4.6
resources.description: Security+ lesson on authentication factors and how combining them into multifactor authentication strengthens logins.
keyPoints: Explains factor categories: know, have, are
Covers common MFA methods and their trade-offs
Exam-aligned overview of multifactor authentication

resources.title: More Than a Password: Understanding Multifactor Authentication
resources.description: CISA explains what MFA is, the three factor categories, and why phishing-resistant FIDO authentication is the strongest option.
keyPoints: MFA is a layered approach requiring more than one verification method
Factors: something you know, something you have, something you are
FIDO/WebAuthn blocks logins on fake sites, so CISA recommends it most strongly
Number matching helps against push-fatigue where FIDO isn't yet possible

resources.title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B: Authentication and Lifecycle Management
resources.description: The US federal standard for authenticators; Rev. 4 sets the modern password rules many organisations now follow.
keyPoints: Passwords used alone: minimum 15 characters; within MFA: minimum 8
Verifiers SHALL NOT impose composition rules such as mixed character types
No forced periodic changes; force a change only on evidence of compromise
Check new passwords against a blocklist; allow password managers and paste
Passwords are explicitly not phishing-resistant

resources.title: Password managers
resources.description: NCSC advice on why password managers help people keep a unique strong password for every account.
keyPoints: Password managers store passwords so each service can have a unique one
They generate strong passwords and autofill only on the real site, helping against phishing
Turn on 2-step verification, including on the password manager itself
Passkeys are recommended as a safer alternative where available

resources.title: What is a Passkey?
resources.description: The standards body behind passkeys explains how they replace passwords with device-held key pairs.
keyPoints: A passkey is a FIDO credential unlocked with the device's biometric, PIN or pattern
Uses a public/private key pair; the private key never leaves the user's device
Synced passkeys roam via credential managers; device-bound ones stay on one device/key
Described as resistant to phishing and credential stuffing

resources.title: Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet
resources.description: OWASP distinguishes credential stuffing from brute force and password spraying and lists layered defenses, with MFA first.
keyPoints: Credential stuffing: trying username/password pairs breached from another site
Password spraying: one weak password tried against many accounts
MFA is the most effective defense against these attacks
Other layers: leaked-password checks, CAPTCHA, device fingerprinting, user alerts

stages.title: Networking for Security
stages.description: The networking basics defenders rely on: ports and transport protocols, DNS, firewalls, VPNs and how TLS protects HTTPS traffic.
learningObjectives: Explain what a port is and name common well-known ports (22, 53, 80, 443)
Describe how DNS resolves a domain name to an IP address
Explain how firewalls filter traffic by rules and compare stateful, next-gen and web application firewalls
Describe what TLS/HTTPS and VPNs protect, and their limits

explainBack.question: When you open https://example.com from a café Wi-Fi, what happens with DNS, ports and TLS, and how could a firewall and a VPN each help protect you or the network?
rubric: DNS translates a domain name into an IP address via a recursive resolver querying root, TLD and authoritative nameservers (with caching along the way)
Ports are transport-layer (TCP/UDP) endpoints that identify services; HTTPS uses 443, HTTP 80, DNS 53, SSH 22
TLS provides encryption, authentication (via certificates) and integrity; HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, and a handshake establishes session keys
A firewall allows or blocks traffic based on security rules; stateful firewalls track connections, NGFWs add deep packet inspection and app awareness, WAFs filter HTTP traffic to web apps
A VPN encrypts traffic in a tunnel to the VPN server (useful on public Wi-Fi), but only adds security if you trust the VPN provider

resources.title: Firewall Types - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 3.2
resources.description: Security+ lesson comparing firewall types and where they sit in a network.
keyPoints: Compares traditional and next-generation firewalls
Covers web application firewalls
Explains filtering by ports, protocols and applications

resources.title: What is a computer port? | Ports in networking
resources.description: Explains ports as virtual endpoints that let one device handle many services, with a table of common port numbers.
keyPoints: A port is a virtual point where network connections start and end
Ports work at layer 4 with TCP and UDP; IP addressing is at layer 3
Common ports: 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP
Firewalls typically block ports that aren't needed

resources.title: What is DNS? | How DNS works
resources.description: Walks through a DNS lookup from the recursive resolver through root, TLD and authoritative nameservers.
keyPoints: DNS translates domain names into IP addresses
Recursive resolver handles the client's query
Root -> TLD -> authoritative nameserver returns the IP
Answers are cached in the browser and OS to speed lookups

resources.title: What is a firewall?
resources.description: Defines a firewall as rule-based traffic control between trusted and untrusted networks and surveys firewall types.
keyPoints: A firewall monitors and controls traffic based on security rules
Stateful firewalls use connection context
NGFWs add deep packet inspection and application awareness
WAFs filter HTTP traffic to protect web applications

resources.title: What is TLS (Transport Layer Security)?
resources.description: Explains what TLS does, how it relates to SSL and HTTPS, and what happens in the handshake.
keyPoints: TLS provides encryption, authentication and integrity
HTTPS is TLS encryption on top of HTTP
TLS evolved from SSL; current version is TLS 1.3
Handshake negotiates ciphers, checks certificates and sets session keys

resources.title: What is a VPN?
resources.description: Explains how a VPN encrypts traffic to a VPN server and where its protection ends.
keyPoints: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a VPN server
Useful on public Wi-Fi and for remote access to business networks
Adds security only if you trust the VPN provider
Many organisations are moving to SASE/zero trust instead of VPNs

stages.title: Common Threats & Defenses
stages.description: How phishing, social engineering, malware and ransomware work at a conceptual level, and the layered defenses that stop or limit them.
learningObjectives: Recognise warning signs of phishing and the correct way to respond and report
Explain an organisation's layered defenses against phishing
Distinguish common malware types: virus, worm, trojan, spyware, rootkit, ransomware
Describe defenses against ransomware, especially offline backups

explainBack.question: An employee gets an urgent email asking them to 'verify your account' via a link. Explain the warning signs, what they should do, and how an organisation layers defenses against phishing and the ransomware it might deliver.
rubric: Phishing signs include urgent or emotional pressure, requests for personal or financial data, shortened links and misspelled sender addresses or domains; poor grammar is no longer a reliable sign
Don't click links or attachments; report the message and verify independently through an official website or another channel
Organisational defenses are layered: prevent delivery (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, filtering), user awareness and easy reporting, mitigate impact (MFA, updates), and incident response
A virus activates when an infected file is run, a worm self-replicates across networks without user action, and a trojan hides inside apparently legitimate software
Ransomware encrypts or locks data for payment; key defenses are tested, offline/separate backups plus patching and MFA, and paying gives no guarantee of recovery

resources.title: Phishing - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 2.2
resources.description: Security+ lesson on how phishing and related social engineering techniques trick people.
keyPoints: Explains phishing and its variants
Covers common deception tricks such as spoofed links
Exam-aligned overview of social engineering

resources.title: An Overview of Malware - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 2.4
resources.description: Security+ lesson introducing malware categories and how malware gets onto systems.
keyPoints: Overview of major malware categories
Includes ransomware and how it affects data
Exam-aligned introduction to how malware behaves

resources.title: Recognize and Report Phishing
resources.description: CISA's short public guide to spotting phishing messages and what to do with them.
keyPoints: Signs: urgent or emotional language, requests for personal or financial info
Signs: untrusted shortened URLs and lookalike addresses (amazan.com)
AI makes phishing more polished, so grammar isn't a reliable clue
Recognize, resist, report and delete; verify via official channels

resources.title: Phishing attacks: defending your organisation
resources.description: NCSC's multi-layered approach for organisations, arguing training alone cannot stop phishing.
keyPoints: Layer 1: stop delivery with DMARC, SPF, DKIM and email filtering
Layer 2: help users identify and report phishing without blame
Layer 3: limit impact with MFA, updates and password managers
Layer 4: respond quickly with logging and an incident plan

resources.title: What is malware?
resources.description: Defines malware and the main types such as viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, rootkits and ransomware.
keyPoints: Virus: activates when the infected file or program is run
Worm: self-replicates across networks with no user action
Trojan: malware disguised inside legitimate-looking software
Rootkit hides unwanted changes in the OS; ransomware demands payment

resources.title: Mitigating malware and ransomware attacks
resources.description: NCSC guidance on how organisations prepare for and limit malware and ransomware, centred on offline backups.
keyPoints: Ransomware locks or encrypts data and demands payment, often in crypto
Paying gives no guarantee; law enforcement doesn't condone paying ransoms
Keep regular, tested backups offline and separate from the network
Layer defenses: filtering, patching, MFA on remote access, incident plans

stages.title: Web Application Security
stages.description: The OWASP Top 10 at a concept level, focusing on how broken access control, injection and cross-site scripting arise and how developers prevent them.
learningObjectives: Explain what the OWASP Top 10 is and name its top category
Describe broken access control and how to prevent it
Explain injection (e.g. SQL injection) and the preferred prevention
Explain cross-site scripting and its main defenses

explainBack.question: Explain what the OWASP Top 10 is, then describe broken access control, SQL injection and cross-site scripting: what goes wrong in each and how a developer prevents it.
rubric: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document of the most critical web application security risks; in the 2025 edition Broken Access Control is A01
Broken access control lets users act outside their permissions (e.g. changing an ID in a URL to see another account); prevent it with deny-by-default and server-side enforcement of access checks
Injection happens when untrusted input is sent to an interpreter and executed as commands; the preferred fix is a safe API with parameterized queries, plus server-side input validation and escaping

XSS makes a site run attacker-supplied script in the victim's browser with the site's privileges, because input is included in a page without sanitizing/encoding; OWASP 2025 counts XSS under Injection
XSS defenses include context-aware output encoding (templating frameworks), sanitizing HTML with a library like DOMPurify, and a strict Content Security Policy

resources.title: SQL Injection - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 2.3
resources.description: Security+ lesson explaining conceptually how SQL injection works and why input handling matters.
keyPoints: Explains how untrusted input can alter a database query
Shows the impact of injection on data
Exam-aligned conceptual overview

resources.title: OWASP Top 10:2025
resources.description: The 2025 release of OWASP's awareness list of the most critical web application security risks.
keyPoints: A standard awareness document for developers and web app security
A01:2025 is Broken Access Control
A05:2025 is Injection; A04 is Cryptographic Failures
New 2025 entries include Software Supply Chain Failures

resources.title: A01:2025 Broken Access Control
resources.description: Describes how access control fails (IDOR, forced browsing, privilege escalation) and how to prevent it.
keyPoints: Users act outside their intended permissions
Example: changing an account ID in a URL (IDOR)
Enforce access checks in trusted server-side code
Deny by default and validate record ownership

resources.title: A05:2025 Injection
resources.description: Explains injection flaws, including SQL injection and XSS, and the recommended prevention approach.
keyPoints: Untrusted input sent to an interpreter is executed as commands
Includes SQL, NoSQL, OS command and XSS (CWE-79)
Preferred defense: safe APIs with parameterized queries or ORMs
Add positive server-side input validation and escaping

resources.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
resources.description: MDN explains how XSS bypasses the same-origin policy and the layered defenses developers use.
keyPoints: XSS runs attacker code as if it were part of the target site
Requires attacker input placed in a page without sanitizing
Defense: output encoding via templating frameworks
Defense: sanitize HTML (DOMPurify), Trusted Types, strict CSP

stages.title: Cryptography Basics
stages.description: The building blocks of applied cryptography: symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, hashing vs encryption, salted password hashing, digital signatures and certificates.
learningObjectives: Compare symmetric and asymmetric encryption and give an example algorithm of each
Explain why hashing differs from encryption and why passwords are stored as salted slow hashes
Describe how digital signatures provide integrity, authentication and non-repudiation
Explain what a TLS certificate contains and the role of a certificate authority

explainBack.question: Explain the difference between encryption and hashing, how a website should store passwords, and how digital signatures and certificates let your browser trust a site.
rubric: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for encryption and decryption (e.g. AES); asymmetric uses a public key and a private key (e.g. RSA, ECC)
Hashing is one-way (a fixed-length output that cannot be decrypted), while encryption is reversible with the key
Passwords should be stored with a slow password-hashing algorithm (Argon2id preferred; scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 otherwise) plus a unique random salt per password to defeat precomputed tables
A digital signature is generated with the signer's private key and verified with the public key; it provides integrity, origin authentication and non-repudiation
A TLS certificate holds the domain, the public key, issue/expiry dates and the issuing certificate authority's digital signature; self-signed certificates aren't trusted by browsers

resources.title: Hashing and Digital Signatures - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 1.4
resources.description: Security+ lesson on hash functions, salting and how digital signatures are created and verified.
keyPoints: Explains hashes as fixed-length one-way digests
Covers salting stored password hashes
Shows how signing and verifying use the key pair

resources.title: How NOT to Store Passwords! - Computerphile
resources.description: Computerphile explains why plain text and plain encryption are bad ways to store passwords and why salted hashing is better.
keyPoints: Why storing plaintext or encrypted passwords is dangerous
Why plain hashes are vulnerable to precomputed lookups
How salting and slow hashing improve password storage

resources.title: What is encryption? | Types of encryption
resources.description: Introduces encryption, keys and algorithms, and contrasts symmetric with asymmetric encryption.
keyPoints: Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key
Symmetric: one shared key (AES, 3-DES)
Asymmetric: public key encrypts, private key decrypts (RSA, ECC)
Asymmetric encryption underpins TLS

resources.title: Password Storage Cheat Sheet
resources.description: OWASP's guide to storing passwords safely: hashing not encryption, salting, peppering and recommended algorithms.
keyPoints: Hashing is one-way; encryption is reversible, so passwords should be hashed
A unique random salt per password defeats precomputed tables
Preferred: Argon2id; then scrypt; bcrypt for legacy; PBKDF2 for FIPS
Work factors make each guess slow to compute

resources.title: FIPS 186-5: Digital Signature Standard (DSS)
resources.description: The US federal digital signature standard; its introduction explains how signatures are generated and verified.
keyPoints: The private key generates signatures; only its owner may use it
The public key verifies signatures and need not be secret
Messages are hashed to a fixed-length value before signing
Signatures give integrity, signer authentication and non-repudiation

resources.title: What is an SSL certificate?
resources.description: Explains what an SSL/TLS certificate contains, why sites need one and the role of certificate authorities.
keyPoints: Contains domain, issuing CA and its signature, dates and the public key
Enables encryption and authentication for HTTPS
Issued and digitally signed by a trusted certificate authority
Self-signed certificates are flagged as untrusted by browsers

stages.title: Security Operations
stages.description: How defenders detect and respond: centralised logging and SIEM, the incident response lifecycle as updated by NIST SP 800-61r3, and vulnerability management with CVE and CVSS.
learningObjectives: Explain what a SIEM does and how SOAR builds on it
Describe the incident response lifecycle and how NIST SP 800-61r3 maps it to CSF 2.0
Explain what a CVE is and how CVSS rates severity
Describe the principles of vulnerability management and patching

explainBack.question: A SIEM alert suggests an internet-facing server was compromised through a known vulnerability. Explain how the SOC detects it, the phases of responding, and how CVE/CVSS and patch management fit in.
rubric: A SIEM collects, centralises and analyses log data and raises alerts on suspicious activity; SOAR automates parts of the response using playbooks but doesn't replace human responders
The classic lifecycle (SP 800-61r2) is Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity; SP 800-61r3 (2025) maps these onto the CSF 2.0 Functions
SP 800-61r3 treats lessons learned as continuous improvement shared as soon as identified, not only after recovery

A CVE entry gives a publicly known vulnerability a unique ID, a description and a public reference; CVSS scores severity 0-10 (Low 0.1-3.9, Medium 4.0-6.9, High 7.0-8.9, Critical 9.0-10.0) and measures severity, not risk
Good vulnerability management keeps an asset inventory, applies updates as soon as possible (ideally automatically), and prioritises actively exploited and internet-facing vulnerabilities

resources.title: Incident Response - CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 - 4.8
resources.description: Security+ lesson walking through the phases of the incident response process.
keyPoints: Covers preparation, detection and analysis
Covers containment, eradication and recovery
Covers lessons learned after an incident

resources.title: Implementing SIEM and SOAR platforms: Executive guidance
resources.description: Joint government guidance (May 2025) explaining what SIEM and SOAR platforms do and what leaders should consider before adopting them.
keyPoints: A SIEM collects, centralises and analyses log data
It alerts on activity that may indicate an incident
SOAR automates some responses through predefined playbooks
SOAR complements, not replaces, human responders

resources.title: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management: A CSF 2.0 Community Profile (SP 800-61r3)
resources.description: NIST's April 2025 incident response guidance, which supersedes Rev. 2 and maps incident response onto CSF 2.0.
keyPoints: Supersedes SP 800-61 Rev. 2 (2012)
Rev. 2 phases: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident
Maps those phases to CSF 2.0's Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Lessons learned shared as soon as found, feeding continuous improvement

resources.title: common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) - Glossary | CSRC
resources.description: NIST glossary definitions of CVE, the common naming scheme for publicly known vulnerabilities.
keyPoints: CVE: a list of entries for publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities
Each entry has a unique ID, a description and a public reference
Gives common names to vulnerabilities across tools
The CVE list feeds the National Vulnerability Database

resources.title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System v4.0: Specification Document
resources.description: The CVSS v4.0 specification, defining metric groups and the qualitative severity scale.
keyPoints: CVSS communicates vulnerability severity on a 0-10 scale; it is not a risk measure
Metric groups: Base, Threat, Environmental, Supplemental
Threat and environmental scoring are the consumer's responsibility

resources.title: Vulnerability management
resources.description: NCSC principles for finding, prioritising and fixing vulnerabilities across an organisation.
keyPoints: Default to update: apply updates as soon as possible, ideally automatically
Know your assets and who is responsible for them
Prioritise actively exploited and internet-facing issues
Decisions not to update need senior risk-owner sign-off

stages.title: Governance, Ethics & Careers
stages.description: How security is governed with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, the legal and ethical limits on security testing, and how entry-level careers and certifications are structured.
learningObjectives: Name and describe the six NIST CSF 2.0 Functions and why Govern is central
Explain CSF Profiles and Tiers at a high level
Explain why security testing requires explicit authorisation, using the UK Computer Misuse Act as an example
Describe how the NICE Framework and entry certifications like CompTIA Security+ map to security careers

explainBack.question: Describe the six NIST CSF 2.0 Functions, explain why testing someone else's system without permission is illegal even for 'good' reasons, and outline how someone starts a security career.
rubric: CSF 2.0 (February 2024) has six Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; Govern was added in 2.0 and sits at the center because it informs the other five
The CSF is voluntary and doesn't prescribe how outcomes are achieved; Profiles describe current vs target posture and Tiers (Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive) describe rigor
Under the UK Computer Misuse Act s.1 it is an offence to make a computer perform a function intending to access data when you know the access is unauthorised; good intent is not a defence

A penetration test is commissioned by the system owner to gain assurance by attempting to breach the system with adversary tools and techniques; it shows only that known issues weren't exploitable on the day of the test
The NIST NICE Framework gives a common language of Work Roles, Competency Areas and Task/Knowledge/Skill statements; CompTIA Security+ validates core skills for roles like security analyst

resources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
resources.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology
resources.description: NIST's own introduction to CSF 2.0 and its six Functions.
keyPoints: Introduces the purpose of CSF 2.0
Explains the six Functions including the new Govern
From the agency that publishes the framework

resources.title: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
resources.description: The CSF 2.0 document itself, describing the six Functions, Profiles and Tiers.
keyPoints: Published February 26, 2024
Functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Govern is at the center because it informs the other five
Doesn't prescribe how outcomes are achieved
Tiers: Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive; Profiles: Current and Target

resources.title: Computer Misuse Act 1990, Section 1: Unauthorised access to computer material
resources.description: The statutory text making unauthorised access to computer material a criminal offence in the UK.
keyPoints: Offence: causing a computer to perform a function to access data or programs
Requires knowing the intended access is unauthorised
Intent need not target any particular computer or data
Can carry imprisonment on conviction

resources.title: Penetration testing
resources.description: NCSC guidance on what penetration testing is, how to scope it, and how to use the results.
keyPoints: Pen testing tries to breach a system with adversary techniques to gain assurance
It validates security, like an audit; it isn't the main way to find vulnerabilities
Shows only no known issues were exploitable on the day of the test
Scope changes must be documented; fixing findings stays the client's responsibility

resources.title: NICE Framework Resource Center
resources.description: NIST's hub for the NICE Workforce Framework, the common language for cybersecurity work roles and skills.
keyPoints: Common language for cybersecurity work and required knowledge and skills
Building blocks: Work Roles, Competency Areas, Task/Knowledge/Skill statements
Used for career pathways, training design and hiring

resources.title: CompTIA Security+ Certification
resources.description: CompTIA's official page for Security+, a widely recognised entry-level security certification.
keyPoints: Globally recognised certification for core cybersecurity skills
Targets roles such as security analyst, security engineer and sysadmin
V7 is current; V8 is expected around November 2026 with AI-related risks added

name: Cybersecurity
description: Defensive security fundamentals for an entry-level career: core principles, authentication, networks, threats, web and crypto basics, security operations and governance.
